title: FSSAI Weighs National Ban on Analogue Paneer After State Consensus Push
excerpt: FSSAI chief Rajit Punhani will put a nationwide analogue paneer ban to state food safety commissioners on September 24 — eight states already prohibit it, and the regulator says paneer is nutritionally irreplaceable.
body:
• FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani said the regulator will propose a nationwide ban on analogue paneer at a plenary meeting with food safety commissioners of all states and UTs on September 24, 2026.
  • “Once all the states give us feedback, and if there’s a consensus, then the authorities will also ban analogue paneer across the country,” Punhani told NDTV.
  • Eight states — Punjab, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand — already have bans on analogue paneer.
  • The national move follows a National Human Rights Commission request for clarifications on the products’ composition, health impact and testing.

India’s food regulator is moving to take the fight against fake paneer national. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) CEO Rajit Punhani said the authority will propose a nationwide ban on analogue paneer at a plenary meeting with food safety commissioners of all states and union territories on September 24, 2026 — conditional on state consensus.

“Once all the states give us feedback, and if there’s a consensus, then the authorities will also ban analogue paneer across the country,” Punhani said in an NDTV interview this week, as reported by multiple outlets including eDairy News India, Curly Tales and FoodManifest.

“Once all the states give us feedback, and if there’s a consensus, then the authorities will also ban analogue paneer across the country.”

— Rajit Punhani, CEO, FSSAI

What analogue paneer is — and why paneer is different

Real paneer is a standardised milk-derived product. Analogue paneer replaces some or all of the milk fat and solids with vegetable oils — including hydrogenated oils and palm oil — along with starches, emulsifiers, binding agents and artificial whiteners. It looks and cooks like paneer but is substantially lower in protein and higher in trans and hydrogenated fats, and experts flag raised bad cholesterol, cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

Punhani drew a distinction between paneer and other dairy analogues. While cheese analogues formulated from vegetable fats hold recognised niche markets internationally, he argued, paneer occupies an irreplaceable dietary role across India as a primary staple and fundamental protein source for millions of households — so widespread substitution undermines basic public nutrition while deceiving consumers about what they are eating.

From state bans to a national push

The September 24 proposal did not come out of nowhere. FSSAI’s Central Advisory Committee had already finalised an analogue-paneer-ban proposal in October 2025, formally confirmed on March 2, 2026 under Punhani’s chairmanship. Eight states now have bans covering manufacture, processing, packaging, storage, transportation, distribution and sale. Maharashtra imposed a one-year ban in August 2026; Karnataka followed on August 17.

The national trigger, per BW Retail World, was the National Human Rights Commission seeking clarifications from FSSAI and states on the composition, health impact and testing of these products. The HinduBusinessLine reported Punhani’s remarks on the sidelines of an Illness to Wellness Foundation event on September 3.

Festive-season enforcement

The ban talk comes amid FSSAI’s pre-Diwali enforcement drive. Punhani said the regulator has issued more than one lakh notices in recent months, suspended around 5,000 food licences, seen 600-plus arrests and about 1,900 convictions, with 33,000 penalty cases. E-commerce and quick-commerce platforms have been told to display manufacturing and expiry dates by September 30 — “one of the key concerns is that the date of manufacturing and the date of expiry is not mentioned on e-commerce platforms. We are now nudging them to rectify this issue,” Punhani said.

The same announcement carried draft restrictions on HFSS (high-fat, salt and sugar) food sales within 50 metres of schools. And on August 31, Zomato adopted a zero-tolerance policy on analogue dairy in listed restaurant dishes.

What it means for your plate

The commercial stakes are real. Analogue paneer wholesales at roughly half the price of real paneer, so a national ban would raise raw-material costs for restaurants, caterers, cloud kitchens and street vendors — while being a major win for the organised dairy sector and milk farmers. For consumers, the signal is straightforward: the paneer on your thali should be milk, not palm oil and starch. Whether September 24 delivers a consensus will decide if that becomes the law of the land.
